1: This is the technical deep dive for Book 08 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, D N S, DHCP and eye-pam.
It's for the network and D D I engineers who will design the resolution paths, move authority off Active Directory, and run the result.

Part 1 covers the hard surfaces: split-brain D N S and what Active Directory D N S really carries, the places queries escape agency policy, and the D N S identity and DNSSEC work underneath certificates and tokens.

Part 2 builds and runs the control plane: cloud private endpoints, eye-pam as the authority for address blocks, the reference architecture, then the six-phase migration and the evidence that keeps it honest.
Vendors appear only as the book's examples, never as endorsements.
2: Almost every connection begins with a D N S query, and in a hybrid, multi-cloud agency the answer now decides far more than an address.
nist's 2026 D N S guide says D N S has become a security control, not just a service.
Chapter 01 names six jobs it now does, from publishing private addresses for cloud endpoints to anchoring certificate checks, because revocation endpoints are names too.
Yet most agencies run D N S on as many as five platforms that share no state: on-premises, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and VMware.
The cost shows up on every change.
A new Azure private endpoint can need four more D N S changes, on four consoles, in four syntaxes.
And the forwarding rules that connect those platforms usually belong to no single team.
3: The book quotes the mandates rather than inflating them, and so will I. Read together, they ask for agency-controlled resolvers that log, encrypt, validate, send internet-bound queries through sis-uh's Protective D N S, and can't be routed around.
The slide lists each source, from O M B M twenty-two oh-nine to the logging baseline in M-26-14 and the long-standing DNSSEC requirement.
One point on fed-ramp: it certifies a cloud service, not an architecture, and the agency still authorizes its own system.
A Moderate certification doesn't cover High, and on-premises appliances sit inside the agency's own boundary.
Every chapter follows one sequence: inventory, coexist, migrate authority, federate the clouds, decommission A D D N S and DHCP, then harden and evidence.
Five decisions carry most of the risk, and we'll meet each one along the way.
4: Module 1 is split-brain D N S and leaving Active Directory D N S.
For twenty years A D was quietly the agency's D N S service, and the records it kept for itself don't follow identities to the cloud.
So leaving it is an inventory problem first, finished before the first domain controller retires.
5: Split-brain is the same name returning different answers depending on where the query starts.
The accidental kind is the problem, and with several D N S systems holding copies of the same names, it's close to guaranteed.
The classic example: an Azure storage account with a private endpoint.
A workload in AWS sees the private address only if a forwarding rule sends that name to Azure.
If the rule is missing, the name still resolves, just to the public address, and Microsoft attributes roughly seventy percent of its private-endpoint 403 errors to exactly that.
The same silent drift hits SaaS sign-in paths and security block lists.
Runbooks can't keep up, because nothing errors.
The fix is structural: a control plane.
6: When a domain is deployed, its name becomes a D N S zone, its domain controllers become the authoritative servers, and every domain-joined machine points at them.
Nobody chose that as a D N S architecture, but it is one.
Storing zones in A D brings secure dynamic updates and multi-master operation, and both disappear with the directory.
So the A D D N S estate breaks into seven components, each needing its own decision: integrated zones, file-backed zones, stubs, conditional forwarders, GlobalNames, reverse zones and signed zones.
One correction to the source: conditional forwarders are easy to export, because Windows stores each one as a zone.
The hard part isn't finding them.
It's deciding which of the forwarders built up over the years for partners, trusts and retired systems still matter.
7: Domain controllers advertise themselves through D N S. Netlogon registers a family of SRV and A records, and clients use them to find a domain controller.
Those records are dynamic, changing as controllers and sites change.
Lose them, and the failures are broad: domain join, sign-in and Group Policy break, Kerberos falls back to N T L M or fails, and clients end up at a distant domain controller.

The program builds the inventory from two sources and resolves each critical record from every D N S server and every site, and Chapter 10 makes thirty days of clean resolution a gate for decommissioning.
Because these records need secure registration from domain controllers, they stay on A D D N S or a D D I platform that accepts it until the last controller goes.
Azure Private D N S can't host them.
8: Clients keep their own D N S records current through dynamic update, and the secure version records an owner for each name, so only that owner can change it.
That only exists in A D-integrated zones.
The DHCP server is part of this, and a handful of settings decide whether the records stay trustworthy.
For example, the DHCP server that registers a name becomes its owner, so failover partners must share the same D N S credential, ideally one dedicated standard account.
Name protection stops one client overwriting another's name.
And without scavenging, D N S becomes a map of where devices used to be; Microsoft documents that mismatched scavenging and lease times can send one computer's Kerberos tickets to another.
These settings are rarely documented outside the servers, so they belong in the inventory.
9: Microsoft's path is a phased move toward cloud-first, not an all-at-once decommission, and A D itself isn't deprecated.
What changes is where the D N S records come from.
Entra ID publishes no zones and no locator records.
Entra-joined devices use tokens; hybrid-joined devices still look for a domain controller, and Kerberos survives in pockets.
Here's the failure to recognize: resolve a name to the wrong host, and a valid ticket for computer A gets presented to computer B, which rejects it.
It looks like an identity problem, but the cause is D N S.
So before any domain controller goes, keep locator records resolvable until every consumer is token-based, test and prune the forwarders, and move each remaining zone type by its own method.
10: Module 2 covers edge interception, D N S identity and DNSSEC.
Every policy control assumes the query reaches it, so we'll look at three ordinary ways it doesn't, none of which reports.
Then why a perfectly valid certificate can still fail because of D N S, and finally DNSSEC.
11: SD-WAN edges can intercept D N S no matter which resolver a client was given.
In the book's Cisco example, that's the redirect-dns action.
The point of this slide is that the destination decides whether agency policy applies at all.

Sent to an agency resolver, the query gets block lists, validation and logging, and internet lookups leave through Protective D N S. Sent to an outside resolver, it gets none of that, and nothing alerts.
The feature has limits too; it handles only IPv4 over UDP, for instance.
Two refinements: the target must be a server the edge can address, not a loopback agent on a laptop.
And even a fed-ramp-listed sassy resolver bypasses the agency's own plane, so the redirect target is always the agency resolver, with any sassy resolver behind it.
12: The most common bypass is the endpoint itself, sending encrypted D N S straight to a public resolver.
Federal policy wants encrypted D N S, but terminated at agency resolvers or Protective D N S.
Each transport gives you a different handle.
Plain D N S can be redirected.
D N S over TLS or QUIC can be blocked except to approved resolvers.
D N S over HTTPS hides inside ordinary web traffic, so an edge-only design can't govern it.
On Windows, add the agency's resolvers to the known DoH list, and note that since June 2026 the Windows Server 2025 D N S Server accepts client DoH, though its upstream stays unencrypted.
Browsers resolve names themselves, so the program adopts sis-uh's browser configuration as mandatory policy.
13: The third bypass sits on the access layer.
A rogue DHCP server handing out a malicious resolver can move a whole subnet onto an attacker's D N S in one step, past every block list.
In IPv6, rogue router advertisements do the same, and they're often the bigger surface, because many networks don't govern them at all.
Other DHCP options steer traffic too, like the search list and the proxy setting.
The Windows safeguard is narrower than it looks: it stops a misconfigured Windows server, not a home router plugged into a wall port.
That takes DHCP snooping and RA Guard on the switches, central option management, and eye-pam so an unexpected lease is visible at once.
And since prevention is never complete, watch for hosts whose queries never reach the governed logs.
14: D N S identity, the authoritative mapping of names to addresses and owners, is the first link in the trust chain.
Certificates, policies and tokens all name their subject by FQDN and trust D N S to get the caller there.
Moving to Entra ID tokens removes the domain controller but adds names that must resolve consistently, like the right sign-in endpoint for the cloud you're in.
Here's the certificate version of split-brain: a CA's revocation names exist only in A D D N S, and a cloud caller can't resolve them.
One client breaks the handshake, another quietly skips the check, nothing is logged, and the ticket goes to the P K I team.
And for regional naming, certificate wildcards are narrow, so use per-region names instead.
15: DNSSEC lets a resolver verify that an answer is authentic.
It doesn't encrypt anything; nist is explicit that DNSSEC and encrypted D N S are complements.
Federal policy has required DNSSEC for agency domains since 2009.
On internal zones, nist's new guidance is more cautious than the whitepaper was: signing them is likely of limited value, and recommended against unless required.
So the program signs external zones always, validates on every agency resolver, and signs internal zones only where the system's authorization requires it.
Windows Server's default zone-signing key is below nist's floor, so the program uses stronger keys.
And Azure D N S and Route 53 sign public zones only, so neither gives the agency validation it controls.
16: Operating DNSSEC is mostly key management, automated and audited.
nist recommends a hardware security module for the important keys, signatures valid for about five to seven days, and it prefers ECDSA, because smaller keys keep responses small.
The slide has the full parameters.
Moving a signed zone has its own careful sequence, run in Phase 3.
Don't start a key rollover during the move.
Keep the old signing until the new chain validates from an independent checker, and only then stop signing at the source.
Watch the validators, because clients only see generic failures.
An A D-signed internal zone moving to Azure Private D N S, which can't sign, is a documented risk decision.
And retire old trust anchors after the ninety-day validation period.
17: Part 2 builds and runs the control plane, starting with Module 3, the design.
Every cloud ships its own private D N S and its own address manager, and unless one plane governs both, names and addresses drift apart one console at a time.
18: Each cloud ships its own private D N S, with its own console, API, zone model and failure behavior, and none was designed to share policy with the others.
The slide compares AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and VMware NSX.
Azure private endpoints are the most common source of split-brain, so they get the detail.
The private answer only comes back from a resolver that can see a linked private zone.
D N S answers don't grant access; the service's network setting does.
Use one zone per service type everywhere, with Microsoft's recommended names.
And watch the NXDOMAIN trap: a partner's storage account can lead into your empty zone and fail, which is fixed by enabling fallback to internet on the zone's link.
19: Two rules turn Azure private endpoints into something governed.

Every resolver outside Azure, on-premises, in other clouds and at branches, forwards each service's public zone, not the privatelink zone, to the Private Resolver's inbound endpoint or an agency resolver that does.
Azure Government uses different names, so a design spanning both clouds needs both sets.
Second, build the resolver in the hub as a forwarding bridge, not an authority, so on-premises D N S reaches it by conditional forwarding, never delegation.
The slide carries the sizing limits.
The traps are worth remembering: don't link a ruleset to the network its own rule points at, or it loops, and don't list a custom resolver beside Azure's built-in one.
20: The address side has the same problem as the name side.
Every cloud and NSX allocates addresses on its own, so a range created in a console can overlap on-premises space or another division, and nobody knows until a conflict appears.
AWS can hand authority for private address scopes to an external eye-pam, with Infoblox as the book's example, but not in GovCloud, so it doesn't help a GovCloud estate today.
Azure and Google Cloud can't hand off, so you mirror and reconcile.
The rule: reserve blocks in the enterprise eye-pam before any cloud or NSX network is created, integrate where you can, reconcile where you can't, and monitor sync health.
And plan IPv4 and IPv6 together.
21: Chapter 08's architecture is simple to draw.
A branch query goes through the SD-WAN edge to an agency resolver, into the policy plane, and on to each cloud's private zones, while internet lookups leave through sis-uh's Protective D N S.
Five decisions carry almost all of the operational risk, and each fails silently: the query still resolves, just outside policy or to the wrong address.
They are the redirect-dns destination, the order of the forwarding chain, per-cloud conditional forwarding, the A D D N S inventory, and reachability of the certificate revocation endpoints.
Each has a check you run in the live configuration, not the design document, before the next SD-WAN or D D I change.
For example, resolve one name per namespace from every origin; a public address means a missing rule.
22: The policy plane isn't one box.
It has three parts: an on-premises D N S and DHCP layer that replaces A D D N S, a management plane holding the system of record, and local resolvers that keep answering if management is unreachable.
It overlays the cloud services; it doesn't replace them.
Changes converge in seconds, not milliseconds, so an emergency block has to be verified where clients are served.
Infoblox is the book's example, and its government cloud offering is certified at Moderate.
The architecture stays the same in federal clouds; authorization and integrations change.
A Moderate plane doesn't cover High systems, so use a service authorized at the right level, or keep the plane inside the agency's boundary.
The slide lists the other government-cloud gaps.
23: Module 4 is the migration and running the plane.
Name resolution has to keep working while its authority moves, so Chapter 10 makes the migration a series of small, reversible cutovers, each proven from every origin before the next starts.
Then Chapter 11 covers operations and evidence.
24: Here's the book's sequence applied to moving off A D D N S and DHCP onto one policy plane.
Six phases: inventory, coexistence, migrating authority, cloud federation, decommissioning, and hardening.
Each one ends with a rollback point and a consistency test, not a calendar date.
The playbook's durations are planning estimates; the gates decide.
And every move of authority runs the same loop.
Export, transform and import with a dry run.
Switch authority one mechanism at a time.
Wait until no client queries the old server.
Then restore the TTL and file the evidence.
If a check fails, you revert the switch, and the old authority, still intact, answers again.
25: Phase 1 is read-only, so it carries no rollback risk, but anything it misses can't be repaired later.
It collects every zone, record, forwarder, DHCP scope and resolution path, including the health of the data, because stale records migrate as faithfully as good ones.
Then each component gets a target and a method.
Internal zones move to the new platform.
External zones need a registrar change, so they're high risk.
And locator records stay where domain controllers can register, because there's no Azure-native equivalent.
Phase 2 adds the new resolvers without moving authority, forwarding both ways, with exactly one authoritative path per namespace so queries don't loop.
Two errors cause most failures here, and the slide names both.
26: Phase 3 is where zones, forwarders, DHCP scopes and clients actually move, each move one pass through the cutover loop.
Records move, then you observe for at least thirty days, with the old copy left in place as the rollback point.
Three patterns cover almost every zone, and each has its own rollback.
Check the record types that behave differently on the new platform; SRV records are the most consequential and the most underestimated, because nothing moves them when A D retires.
DHCP moves scope by scope, with its options, and failover stays on throughout.
One trap to plan for: removing a network link from an Azure private zone deletes its auto-registered records, and Microsoft says they can't be restored.
27: Phase 4 brings each cloud under the plane, and its real contribution is the validation matrix: every class of name resolves correctly from every origin.
A private endpoint name returning a public address from anywhere is a failed test, even if the application seems to work.
Phase 5 is the one step whose mistakes can't be cheaply undone, so it's gated, not scheduled.
All five gates must pass, including locator records resolving at one hundred percent for thirty consecutive days, and ninety days of parallel running with no critical alerts.
Then decommission in order, archiving the final exports before anything is removed, with a seven-day burn-in.
Losing locator records early causes forest-wide sign-in and domain-join failures.
28: A single policy plane only works if divisions can still run their networks through it, because a division that can't will work around it.
So each division gets its own scope, with manager, operator and auditor roles, and no visibility outside it.
Whatever stays on Windows or Azure needs the same discipline, including locks on critical zones.
Every object should sit behind one documented API, so automation, ticketing and pipelines share the same roles and audit trail.
M-26-14 doesn't name D N S or DHCP, but its baseline needs network address information, searchable for six months and retrievable for a year.
The book's reading is that query logs and lease history supply exactly that.
Last, how to keep it all honest.
29: Last, keeping it honest during and after the hybrid period.
Chapter 11's troubleshooting reference covers the common failures.
For example, a private endpoint returning its public address usually means an unlinked zone, a bad forwarder target or a timeout that's too short.
Then watch continuously: resolve the locator records every fifteen minutes from every site, detect drift between platforms, and commit each report so the history is evidence.
The evidence checklist opens with the five decisions, each checked live.

So, before the next SD-WAN or D D I change: audit every branch's redirect target, verify the chain order, finish the A D D N S inventory before touching a domain controller, confirm the sovereign-cloud limits, and take open questions to the vendors.
